# 2026-11-21: Parts with several coordinates, and branching bodies {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" icon="false"}
**Status:** exploratory · **Thread:** T2 · **Checked by:** `tests/test_chain.py`
:::

**Question.** The [note on chains](2026-11-21-chains.qmd) gave a rule for one coordinate:
push on the part, and each internal damper costs its damping times the square of its
stretch per unit motion of the contact point. What if the part has several coordinates,
such as two masses at once? And what changes when the body branches, like a leg on a
trunk that carries other legs?

**Short answer.** A part with several coordinates gets to choose how it is pushed. Its
effective contact damping is $b_c$ plus the cost of the *best* pattern of forces on its
coordinates. Two consequences follow:

- *Groups of nodes.* At low frequency, a group of nodes in a chain holds exactly what its
    node nearest the contact holds. In band the farther nodes do add something: on the
    uniform chain, node 1 alone holds 38% of the body's information and nodes 1 and 7
    together hold 50%.
- *Branching bodies.* What matters statically is the path from the contact to the part.
    Damping in side branches, such as swing legs, costs nothing at low frequency and
    still costs something in band. On a toy leg with a trunk, heavier damping in the
    swing legs lowers the trunk's share from 0.242 to 0.214 and leaves its static value
    unchanged.

Underneath both is one fact: if an element is the only connection between the contact
side and the part, everything on the contact side costs the same for every part beyond it.

## Setting

As in the chain note: symmetric $H$, $K$, $D$, independent dampers
$D=b_cJ^\top J+\sum_jb_ja_ja_j^\top$, and dynamic stiffness $Z=K-\omega^2H+i\omega D$. A part
now has $m$ coordinates, $y=Pq$ with $P$ an $m\times n$ matrix. By @prp-share-basic(e)
of the propagation note, velocities add nothing, so positions are enough. A *force
pattern* on the part is a vector $\phi\in\mathbb C^m$; it applies the generalized force
$P^\top\phi$, and the body responds with $x(\phi)=Z^{-1}P^\top\phi$.

## Results

::: {#thm-best-pattern name="The part chooses how it is pushed"}
$$
b_{\rm eff}(\omega)=b_c+\min_{\phi}\ \sum_jb_j\,\frac{|a_j^\top x(\phi)|^2}{|J\,x(\phi)|^2},
$$
the minimum taken over patterns that move the contact point. With $W=Z^{-1}P^\top$,
$h=W^\top J^\top$, $s_j=W^\top a_j$ and $N=\sum_jb_js_js_j^*$, the minimum equals
$1/(h^*N^+h)$ and is reached at $\phi=\overline{N^+h}$. If $h$ lies outside the range of
$N$, some pattern moves the contact point without stretching any internal damper, the
minimum is 0, and $b_{\rm eff}=b_c$.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Step 1: reciprocity.* The part's response to the contact force is $PZ^{-1}J^\top$ and to
damper $j$'s noise force $PZ^{-1}a_j$. $Z^{-1}$ is symmetric, so these are
$W^\top J^\top=h$ and $W^\top a_j=s_j$. For any pattern, $h^\top\phi=JW\phi=Jx(\phi)$
and $s_j^\top\phi=a_j^\top x(\phi)$.

*Step 2: the definition.* The part receives internal noise $M=2\sigma_T^2N$, so
$q=h^*M^+h=h^*N^+h/(2\sigma_T^2)$ and $b_{\rm eff}-b_c=1/(2\sigma_T^2q)=1/(h^*N^+h)$.

*Step 3: Cauchy-Schwarz.* $N$ is Hermitian and positive semidefinite. If $h$ is in its
range, then $h=N^{1/2}(N^{+})^{1/2}h$, and for any $\psi$
$$
|h^*\psi|^2=\big|\big((N^+)^{1/2}h\big)^*\,N^{1/2}\psi\big|^2\le(h^*N^+h)\,(\psi^*N\psi),
$$
with equality at $\psi=N^+h$. So $\max_\psi|h^*\psi|^2/(\psi^*N\psi)=h^*N^+h$. If $h$ is
outside the range, take $\psi$ in the null space of $N$ with $h^*\psi\ne0$: the ratio is
unbounded, and $q=\infty$ as in @def-beff of the propagation note.

*Step 4: back to patterns.* Put $\psi=\bar\phi$. Then $|h^*\psi|=|h^\top\phi|=|Jx|$ and
$\psi^*N\psi=\sum_jb_j|s_j^\top\phi|^2=\sum_jb_j|a_j^\top x|^2$. The maximum of the ratio
in Step 3 is one over the minimum cost.
:::

For one coordinate there is only one pattern, and the theorem reduces to
@thm-reciprocity of the chain note. Two consequences come straight from the minimum:

- *More coordinates never hurt.* Adding coordinates to the part enlarges the set of
    patterns, so the minimum can only fall. This is a second proof of
    @prp-share-basic(b).
- *When a part holds everything.* If some pattern moves the contact point without
    stretching any internal damper, the part holds the whole body's information at that
    frequency. For the whole body every force is allowed, so this is possible exactly
    when $J^\top$ is not in the span of the $a_j$, the condition of @prp-contact. The
    SEA's rotor and link together hold everything: push both so that they move
    together, and the series damper never stretches.

The formula matches the state-space $b_{\rm eff}$ to $4\times10^{-11}$ on random chains
with parts of two or three nodes. In 200 random patterns per case, none did better than
the predicted best, which reaches the minimum to $10^{-10}$ (`check_matrix_reciprocity`).

::: {#prp-group-static name="A group holds statically what its nearest node holds"}
In a chain with a free far end, let $S$ be a set of nodes and $s$ its node nearest the
contact. Then $\rho_S(0)=\rho_s(0)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
At $\omega=0$ apply forces $\phi_i$ at the nodes $i\in S$, with total $F=\sum_i\phi_i\ne0$.
The segment beyond element $j$ is free, so element $j$ carries the sum of the forces
beyond it, $F_j=\sum_{i\in S,\,i>j}\phi_i$, and stretches by $F_j/k_j$. The contact spring
carries $F$, so the contact point moves $F/k_c$. The cost is
$k_c^2\sum_jb_j|F_j|^2/(k_j^2|F|^2)$.

- For $j<s$, every node of $S$ lies beyond element $j$, so $F_j=F$. These terms give
    $k_c^2\sum_{j<s}b_j/k_j^2$ whatever the pattern.
- For $j\ge s$ the terms are nonnegative, and they all vanish when the whole force is put
    at node $s$.

So the minimum is $k_c^2\sum_{j<s}b_j/k_j^2$, the static cost of node $s$ alone
(@prp-static).
:::

Statically, a farther node gives the group nothing, because its forces must pass through
every damper the nearest node's forces pass through. In band it can help: the far node
lets the part cancel some of the backflow. On the uniform chain of the chain note, node 1
holds 0.381 of the body's information, node 7 holds 0.242, and the two together hold
0.499. Nodes 6 and 7 together hold 0.283, against 0.220 and 0.242 alone (`check_pairs`).
The static law for groups holds on random chains to $4\times10^{-11}$
(`check_set_static_law`).

::: {#prp-bridge name="Everything before a bridge costs the same"}
Call an element a *bridge* if removing it splits the body into a side $C$ that contains
the contact node and a side $F$, with the element the only connection between them (no
spring, damper or mass coupling otherwise). Let $c\in C$ and $f\in F$ be its two nodes.
For every force pattern applied on nodes of $F$, the cost
$|a_j^\top x|^2/|Jx|^2$ of each damper inside $C$, and of the bridge's own damper, is the
same.
:::

::: {.proof}
The forces act only on $F$, so the rows of $Zx=$ (force) for the nodes of $C$ have zero on
the right. In those rows, $F$ appears only through the bridge, in row $c$, as
$Z_{cf}x_f$ with $Z_{cf}=-(k_e+i\omega b_e)$. So
$$
Z_{CC}\,x_C=-Z_{cf}\,x_f\,e_c ,\qquad x_C=-Z_{cf}\,x_f\,Z_{CC}^{-1}e_c .
$$
Every motion on the contact side is a fixed multiple of $x_f$, and so is the bridge's
stretch $x_c-x_f$. Every ratio of these motions to the contact motion $x_0$ is therefore
fixed. $Z_{CC}$ is invertible for $\omega>0$: if $Z_{CC}v=0$, the imaginary part of
$v^*Z_{CC}v$ is $\omega\,v^*D_{CC}v=0$. That forces $v_0=0$ through the contact damper,
and equal motion across every damper of the connected side $C$, so $v=0$.
:::

This gives the general form of the chain note's accumulation result:
$$
b_{\rm eff}=b_c+\underbrace{\text{(cost of the contact side)}}_{\text{same for every part beyond}}
+\min_{\phi}\,\text{(cost of the far side)} .
$$
In a chain every element is a bridge. In a tree, every element on the path from the
contact to the part is one. On the leg-on-trunk body below, the hip-trunk element is a
bridge, and the costs of the three dampers up to and including it agree to
$3\times10^{-15}$ across single nodes and 20 random patterns beyond it
(`check_bridge`).

::: {#prp-tree-static name="In a tree, only the path matters statically"}
In a body whose elements form a tree, with only the contact node attached to the ground,
$$
\rho_k(0)=\frac{b_c}{b_c+k_c^2\sum_{j\in\text{path}(k)}b_j/k_j^2},
$$
where $\text{path}(k)$ holds the elements between the contact and node $k$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Apply a static unit force at node $k$. Every branch off the path ends in free nodes, so it
is unloaded and its elements do not stretch. Every element on the path carries the whole
force and stretches by $1/k_j$, and the contact point moves $1/k_c$. @thm-reciprocity of
the chain note then gives the formula.
:::

## A leg on a trunk

The toy body is one-dimensional and vertical. The foot (0.2 kg) is on the ground, with
$k_c=10^5$ N/m and $b_c=270$ N s/m (15% of critical on the total mass). The knee
(0.5 kg), hip (1 kg) and trunk (5 kg) follow, joined by springs of $2\times10^4$,
$2\times10^4$ and $5\times10^4$ N/m. Two identical swing legs hang from the trunk, each a
knee (0.5 kg) and a foot (0.2 kg) on $2\times10^4$ N/m springs. Every element is damped at
5% of critical on its lighter mass, and the swing legs at either 5% or 20%.

| Node | foot | knee | hip | trunk | swing knee | swing foot |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| share, swing legs at 5% | 0.957 | 0.525 | 0.241 | 0.242 | 0.076 | 0.073 |
| share, swing legs at 20% | 0.957 | 0.525 | 0.239 | 0.214 | 0.044 | 0.037 |
| static $\rho(0)$, 5% | 1 | 0.631 | 0.398 | 0.352 | 0.265 | 0.230 |
| static $\rho(0)$, 20% | 1 | 0.631 | 0.398 | 0.352 | 0.153 | 0.112 |

: Share of the body's information held by each node of the leg-on-trunk body (finite window, 100 Hz band), and the static values, which match @prp-tree-static to $6\times10^{-11}$ (`check_tree`). The whole body holds 47.22 bits in both cases. {#tbl-tree}

- *The whole body does not notice the swing legs.* It holds 47.22 bits with either swing
    damping, because the ceiling depends only on the contact damper (@prp-contact).
- *Statically, the trunk does not notice them either.* Its static value is 0.352 in both
    cases, as @prp-tree-static says: the swing legs are off its path.
- *In band, the trunk does notice.* Heavier swing damping lowers the trunk's share from
    0.242 to 0.214. The swing legs ring and feed their dampers' noise back into the trunk.
    The hip, one element farther from the swing legs, barely changes (0.241 to 0.239).
- *The trunk holds as much as the hip.* The hip-trunk spring is stiff and the trunk is
    heavy, so in band the trunk's share (0.242) matches the hip's (0.241). Statically the
    trunk still pays for one more damper on its path.

## What this changes

Thread T2 now has a complete rule for linear bodies: push on the part in the best way,
and add up what each internal damper costs. The path from the contact to the part
decides the static picture. Everything off the path, such as side branches and the far
side of the part, matters only in band, through backflow. For legged robots this
separates two design questions: what lies on the path from the foot to the part that
must hold the force, and how much ringing the rest of the body sends back.

## Limits of this note

- Linear bodies with symmetric $H$, $K$, $D$ and independent viscous dampers.
- The leg-on-trunk body is a one-dimensional toy with one foot on the ground. With two
    feet down the body is no longer a tree, the two contacts share the force, and
    @prp-tree-static no longer applies as stated.
- Gyroscopic terms would break the symmetry that reciprocity needs.
